title: What a Staff Engineer Does, Now That AI Handles the Routine Stuff
summary: What a staff engineer does when AI writes the routine code: cross-team architecture, real mentoring, and knowing when to stop the model.
body_markdown:
Your team ships more code than it did a year ago. Most of it starts in a coding agent, gets a quick review, and merges. The tickets close faster, the board looks healthy, and yet the system feels harder to reason about every month.


That gap, between how fast code gets written and how well anyone understands where it's taking the system, is where the staff engineer has always worked, and coding agents have made it a lot wider.


## **What is a staff engineer, in plain terms**


A staff engineer is an individual contributor with no direct reports and a scope bigger than one team: the technical problems that cross service boundaries, the decisions that are expensive to undo, and the standards everyone else builds on.


If that sounds vague, here's a simpler test. A senior engineer is the person you want on a hard problem. A staff engineer is the person who notices which problem is the hard one, often before anyone has opened a ticket for it.


## **Staff engineer vs senior engineer: it's about scope**


Plenty of senior engineers write better code than the staff engineer down the hall, so code quality won't tell you which role someone is in.


What sets the role apart is how far your judgment reaches: a staff engineer makes the decisions several teams live with, and answers for them when they age badly.


## **What coding agents changed about the job**


Coding agents now write a lot of the routine code: the CRUD endpoint, the migration, the test scaffolding, the boilerplate that used to fill an afternoon. That part of the job got cheap, and it left more decisions behind. When a team can produce much more code, it also gets many more chances to add a dependency nobody needed, a pattern that contradicts the one next door, or a shortcut that holds up until the traffic doubles.


So what's scarce now is someone with enough context, across enough of the system, to say which of those changes matter.


## **The week four caches showed up**


Here's what that looks like on a normal week.


Four teams are working on four different features. Each one hits the same slow call to the customer API, and each one asks its agent how to fix it.


Each agent suggests a cache. Each PR is clean, tested, and reviewed by someone competent. All four merge.


Every one of those reviews was reasonable, and the company now has four caches over the same customer data, with four different expiry rules. The first time support updates a customer's address, every screen that reads from one of those caches keeps showing the old one until it expires.


No single PR review was going to catch this, because the problem lives in the space between four PRs. Catching it is staff work: it means knowing what the other teams are doing, recognizing the pattern on the second cache instead of the fifth, and having the standing to say "let's stop and fix the slow call once."


## **What a staff engineer does day to day**


### **Decides architecture across teams**


Most technical decisions are cheap to reverse, and a good staff engineer lets teams make those fast. Their time goes to the few that aren't: the data model other services will depend on, the boundary between two systems, the vendor you'll be migrating away from in three years.


For those, the job is to compare real options, pick one, write down why, and still own it at the postmortem if it goes wrong.


### **Mentors with real judgment**


When half the code in a PR came from an agent, the diff stops showing how the person thinks. A clean implementation might mean they understood the problem, or that they accepted the first suggestion that passed the tests.


So mentoring moves away from the syntax and toward questions like "what else did you consider, and why not that?" The staff engineer's job is to teach people the reasoning behind the rules, so they can spot the agent's mistakes on their own, including the ones nobody wrote a rule for.


It also matters beyond your own team. With fewer juniors getting hired, someone has to grow the next generation of seniors, a question we dug into in[Senior Devs Aren't Replacing Juniors. They're Replacing Entire Teams](https://www.howdylatam.com/blog/senior-devs-ai-replacing-teams-not-juniors) .


### **Knows when to trust the model, and when to stop it**


Every senior engineer makes this call on their own PRs. A staff engineer makes it for the team: which parts of the codebase an agent can change with a normal review, which ones need a human who knows the history, which tests have to exist before agent-written changes touch billing or auth.


And sometimes it means stopping things outright. Pausing a rollout, reverting a migration that looks fine on paper, or saying "we're not letting the agent refactor this module until someone writes down why it's shaped like this." Making that call stick takes a track record of having been right about this kind of thing before.


## **What years alone don't give you**


You can be a strong senior engineer for fifteen years without ever doing staff work, and there's nothing wrong with that. Plenty of people love going deep on their team's problems and have no interest in the rest.


But if you're trying to tell the two apart, in yourself or someone else, look for evidence of reach:


- Other teams ask this person before they make a big call, without anyone telling them to.
- They can name a decision they changed or prevented, and explain the cost of the alternative.
- Their reasoning is written down somewhere other people actually read.
- When they say "stop," people stop, because the last few times they were right.


Each of those comes from making decisions with consequences beyond your own code, and sticking around to see how they turned out.


## **Back to the four caches**


Go back to those four caches for a moment. Whoever caught the second one before the third team opened its PR, and got all four teams to fix the slow call once, was doing staff work, whatever their title said at the time.


If you've been wondering how to grow into the role, Oscar Mariani and Jonathan Muszkat cover the path in[How to Become a Staff Engineer](https://www.howdylatam.com/blog/how-to-become-a-staff-engineer-strategies-and-insider-tips) . And for the individual version of the same skill, judging an agent's suggestion on your own PR, see[what actually measures a senior engineer now](https://www.howdylatam.com/blog/what-actually-measures-a-senior-engineer-now) .
